prompt:
A variant of merge sort combines its two sorted halves in Θ(n log n) time instead of Θ(n) (for example, by naively re-sorting the combined half with heapsort). What is the overall running time?

Here n is the number of input elements. Big O is an asymptotic upper bound; Θ and Ω denote matching growth and a lower bound.

options.explanation: This would hold if the combine step were linear. Here each level does more than n work.

Correct. Every level still touches all n elements, but now pays an extra logarithmic factor for its piece size. Adding those shrinking logarithmic costs over the logarithmically many levels gives a second logarithmic factor.
The recurrence still halves subproblem sizes, giving logarithmically many levels rather than a quadratic degeneration.

options.text: Θ(n log n log log n)
options.explanation: The extra cost is one full logarithmic factor, rather than a logarithm of a logarithm. Each of about log n levels pays up to about log n per element.

workedExample:
Sum the recursion tree level by level instead of using a formula.

1. The halving still gives about log n levels, and each level's pieces still contain all n elements between them.
2. With a linear combine, each level costs about n. Now each level costs about n times the logarithm of its piece size.
3. At the top the pieces are large, so the extra factor is about log n. One level down it is one less, and so on, down to about 1 at the bottom.
4. Adding those per-level factors (about log n at the top, one less on each level below, down to 1) gives about half the square of log n for every element.

So the running time is Θ(n (log n)²), for n input elements. It shows why the *linear* merge is what makes merge sort optimal: any extra cost in the combine step is paid again on every level.
